When AI Reviews Its Own Code:
Recursive Self-Training Collapse in Code LLMs

Xinyuan Song Affiliation: Emory University, Atlanta, GA, USA    Zekun Cai Affiliation: The University of Tokyo, Tokyo, Japan Affiliation: LocationMind, Tokyo, Japan{xinyuan.song,liang.zhao}@emory.edu, caizekun@csis.u-tokyo.ac.jp    Liang Zhao Affiliation: Emory University, Atlanta, GA, USA
Abstract

Recursive self-training can degrade neural generative models when generated data is reused without fresh human data or external quality control. We study this risk in code LLMs, where AI-generated code can enter real repositories, later become training data, and create a repository-scale self-training loop. While software development traditionally interrupts this loop through pull-request review, tests, compilation, and human approval, AI coding tools now produce code faster than humans can review it, and code review itself is increasingly automated by AI systems. We therefore compare three recursive fine-tuning regimes: no review, Human-gate review using model-independent filters such as compilation and static quality checks, and AI-self-gate review using the code LLM’s own signals such as perplexity and binary self-scoring. Across multiple code LLMs and benchmarks, no review collapses fastest, Human-gate filters slow but do not stop collapse, and AI-self-gate filters can look strong early but later lose their filtering effect. In the clearest case, the binary self-gate enters a rubber-stamp regime where acceptance scores rise while benchmark correctness falls. We explain this behavior by formulating review as gated distributional reweighting, proving that AI self-gating degenerates to ungated self-training under a self-confirming acceptance condition, and giving a spectral analysis of representation-level covariance concentration under recursive retraining. These results suggest that stable recursive code LLM training requires exogenous verification rather than model-coupled self-review. Codes are available at https://github.com/Hik289/code-retraining.git.

1 Introduction

Recursive self-training has been repeatedly shown to be harmful for neural generative models when the loop is not anchored by fresh human data or an external quality signal. In image generation, self-consuming training can reduce distributional variance and drive models toward low-diversity outputs, a failure mode described as model amplification disorder Alemohammad et al. (2023). In general generative modeling, training on recursively generated data can cause model collapse: distributional errors accumulate, low-probability modes are lost, and the learned distribution drifts away from the original data distribution Shumailov et al. (2024); Dohmatob et al. (2024). Similar effects have been reported for language models, where synthetic text can reduce diversity, amplify earlier mistakes, and degrade long-horizon quality unless real data or strong external filtering is preserved in the training loop Briesch et al. (2023); Seddik et al. (2024); Suresh et al. (2025). These results give a general warning: self-training is not automatically self-improvement. When a model is trained on data produced by earlier versions of the same kind of model, the loop can become self-reinforcing rather than corrective.

Code large language models (LLMs) Ben Allal et al. (2023); Li et al. (2023); Rozière et al. (2023); Hui et al. (2024) are likely to face the same risk in a concrete and testable form. A code model can generate programs, add them back into the training corpus, and fine-tune the next model on this synthetic code. If these programs were always correct, diverse, and well reviewed, the loop could cheaply scale code data. In practice, generated code often contains bugs, incomplete logic, repeated templates, missing edge cases, and narrow stylistic patterns. Recursive training can therefore copy these errors into later models, making them better at imitating their own code style while worse at solving programming tasks. This is the recursive self-training trap for code: more data is created, but it can carry the model’s own functional errors into future training.

This issue is no longer only an offline training concern. AI-generated code is rapidly entering real repositories through tools such as GitHub Copilot GitHub (2026b), Cursor Anysphere (2026), Amazon CodeWhisperer Amazon Web Services (2026), and Devin Cognition AI (2026). Studies report large productivity gains from Copilot Peng et al. (2023), and enterprise reports show that Copilot-suggested code is frequently accepted, committed, and merged into pull requests GitHub (2024). Future code LLMs may therefore be trained on repositories already containing AI-generated or AI-assisted code. If such code is collected without review, the loop becomes recursive self-training at repository scale: AI writes code, the code enters GitHub, GitHub enters the next training corpus, and the next model learns from earlier model outputs.

In real software development, code is usually filtered before entering a repository. A developer opens a pull request (PR), and the change may pass through compilation, tests, static analysis, and human review before merging. Modern code review is a lightweight but consequential quality-control process: it catches defects, transfers project knowledge, and affects downstream software quality Bacchelli and Bird (2013); Bosu et al. (2015); McIntosh et al. (2016); Sadowski et al. (2018). This PR process acts as an external quality gate: the author does not define the acceptance rule, and the rule does not become weaker when the author writes worse code. Failed builds, failing tests, or poor design can still block the PR. We call this model-independent acceptance mechanism a Human gate. The term does not require every decision to be manual; it means that the verifier is exogenous to the generator and preserves a fixed quality standard.

The AI coding era weakens this assumption. AI tools can generate PRs faster than humans can review them, while AI code review is becoming a practical engineering workflow. Recent studies examine LLM-assisted review with AI co-reviewers and interactive review assistants Aðalsteinsson et al. (2025); large-scale GitHub Actions analyses show AI review tools automatically commenting on real PRs Sun et al. (2025); and GitHub Copilot code review is now integrated into the PR workflow GitHub (2026a). At the same time, LLM-as-judge systems are known to be sensitive to evaluator design and can favor model-like outputs Zheng et al. (2023); Panickssery et al. (2024). Future repositories may therefore contain both AI-generated and AI-reviewed code. In this setting, the verifier may no longer be a human-quality external process, but another AI model, possibly close to the generator. If AI writes the code and AI reviews the code, the acceptance signal can become coupled to the same distribution being retrained. The review process may look like filtering, but a biased AI reviewer can gradually accept the generator’s degraded outputs as normal.

This observation leads to the central question of this paper: In recursive code LLM training, how do no review, human-style review, and AI-based review differ? Review changes the training distribution: without review, the model trains on all generated outputs; with review, training is reweighted toward samples that satisfy an acceptance rule. The key question is who defines this rule. A Human gate is fixed and model-independent, so it can reject degraded outputs as the generator worsens. An AI self-gate is coupled to the generator, so it can drift with the model and accept degraded model style as high quality. This concern is consistent with evidence that LLM reviewers still miss many human-flagged PR issues, even when they are strong code generators Kumar (2026); Tong and Zhang (2024); Zhao et al. (2025).

We study this question through recursive fine-tuning experiments that directly compare no review, Human-gate review, and AI-self-gate review. The Human-gate setting uses external, model-independent checks to decide which generated code enters future training. The AI-self-gate setting uses the code LLM itself to evaluate its own generated code, so the same model both produces and filters the training data.

We validate this comparison across multiple code LLM families and benchmarks. Our primary experiments use SantaCoder Ben Allal et al. (2023), a 1.1B-parameter code model trained on permissively licensed code from The Stack Kocetkov et al. (2022), and evaluate recursive fine-tuning on HumanEval Chen et al. (2021); OpenAI (2021), MBPP Austin et al. (2021), and LiveCodeBench Jain et al. (2024), with additional results on HumanEval+ and MBPP+ Liu et al. (2024). We further test StarCoder2 Lozhkov et al. (2024), Qwen2.5-Coder Hui et al. (2024), and Code Llama Rozière et al. (2023), with extended vanilla trajectories for StarCoder Li et al. (2023) in the appendix, to examine whether the same pattern holds across model families.

The results show a clear ordering across review regimes: no review collapses fastest, Human-gate filters slow but do not stop collapse, and AI-self-gate filters can look strong early but later lose their filtering effect. In particular, unfiltered recursive fine-tuning degrades all tested model families; Human-gate filters such as compile checks and quality rules reduce the collapse rate but cannot prevent long-horizon semantic drift; and AI-self-gate filters such as perplexity and binary self-scoring become less discriminative as the generator degrades. The binary classifier is the clearest AI-self-gate failure case: acceptance scores rise while benchmark correctness falls, indicating a self-confirming rubber-stamp regime.

Our contributions are summarized as follows:

  1. 1.

    Code LLM self-training collapse: We provide a systematic empirical study of recursive self-training collapse in code LLMs, covering five primary review regimes on SantaCoder, extended appendix trajectories for additional gate variants, and cross-model validation on StarCoder2, Qwen2.5-Coder, and Code Llama.

  2. 2.

    Review as gated reweighting: We formulate review-based recursive training as gated sampling, where generated samples are reweighted by an acceptance function before entering the next round. This explains why useful gates can slow collapse relative to unfiltered self-training.

  3. 3.

    Human gate vs. AI self-gate: We identify exogeneity as the key difference between review regimes: Human gates use fixed, model-independent criteria, while AI self-gates use scores coupled to the generator and can become self-confirming.

  4. 4.

    Theory of collapse and gate failure: We prove that AI self-gate training degenerates to ungated self-training under a self acceptance condition (Theorem 2.3). We also provide a spectral analysis showing representation covariance concentration under recursive retraining (Proposition 2.1).

2 Problem Formulation and Theoretical Analysis

2.1 Iterative Self-Training Without vs. With Gating

Figure 1 illustrates the two recursive training pipelines considered in this paper: ungated self-training, which reuses all generated code, and gated self-training, which filters generated code before retraining. Let x∈𝒳x\in\mathcal{X} denote a prompt or programming task, and let c∈𝒞c\in\mathcal{C} denote a candidate code solution.

No verification (ungated recursion). In ungated recursive self-training, every generated sample is directly reused as training data. The synthetic data distribution at iteration tt is

mtungated​(x,c):=pX​(x)​pθt​(c∣x).m_{t}^{\mathrm{ungated}}(x,c):=p_{X}(x)p_{\theta_{t}}(c\mid x). (2.1)

The next model is obtained by maximum-likelihood estimation (MLE) training on this distribution:

θt+1ungated∈arg⁡maxθ​𝔼(x,c)∼mtungated​[log⁡pθ​(c∣x)].\theta_{t+1}^{\mathrm{ungated}}\in\arg\max_{\theta}\mathbb{E}_{(x,c)\sim m_{t}^{\mathrm{ungated}}}\big[\log p_{\theta}(c\mid x)\big]. (2.2)

Equivalently, this minimizes KL(mtungated∥pXpθ)\mathrm{KL}(m_{t}^{\mathrm{ungated}}\|p_{X}p_{\theta}). Thus, ungated recursion only enforces self-consistency: the next model is trained to imitate the current model’s samples. It does not impose any external constraint on correctness, compilability, or execution success.

Verification (gated recursion). In gated recursive self-training, generated code is accepted only after passing a review or verification signal. Let ℰ⁡(x,c)∈{0,1}\mathcal{E}(x,c)\in\{0,1\} denote the acceptance event, and define

r⁡(x,c):=ℙ⁡(ℰ⁡(x,c)=1∣x,c)∈[0,1].r(x,c):=\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{E}(x,c)=1\mid x,c)\in[0,1]. (2.3)

Here, r⁡(x,c)r(x,c) can represent a compile check, execution test, static quality filter, human review score, or AI-based review score. Conditioning the generator on acceptance gives the accepted distribution

qθt​(c∣x):=ℙ⁡(c∣x,ℰ=1)=pθt​(c∣x)​r​(x,c)Zθt​(x),Zθt​(x):=∑c′∈𝒞pθt​(c′∣x)​r​(x,c′).q_{\theta_{t}}(c\mid x):=\mathbb{P}(c\mid x,\mathcal{E}=1)=\frac{p_{\theta_{t}}(c\mid x)r(x,c)}{Z_{\theta_{t}}(x)},\quad Z_{\theta_{t}}(x):=\sum_{c^{\prime}\in\mathcal{C}}p_{\theta_{t}}(c^{\prime}\mid x)r(x,c^{\prime}). (2.4)

The gated synthetic data distribution is therefore

mtgated​(x,c):=pX​(x)​qθt​(c∣x).m_{t}^{\mathrm{gated}}(x,c):=p_{X}(x)q_{\theta_{t}}(c\mid x). (2.5)

Training on accepted samples yields

θt+1gated∈arg⁡maxθ​𝔼(x,c)∼mtgated​[log⁡pθ​(c∣x)].\theta_{t+1}^{\mathrm{gated}}\in\arg\max_{\theta}\mathbb{E}_{(x,c)\sim m_{t}^{\mathrm{gated}}}\big[\log p_{\theta}(c\mid x)\big]. (2.6)

Thus, gated recursion differs from ungated recursion only through the sampling measure: before training the next model, generated samples are reweighted by the acceptance signal r⁡(x,c)r(x,c).

Difference (see Figures 1). The two recursions differ only in the sampling measure:

mtgated​(x,c)∝mtungated​(x,c)⋅r⁡(x,c).m_{t}^{\mathrm{gated}}(x,c)\propto m_{t}^{\mathrm{ungated}}(x,c)\cdot r(x,c). (2.7)

Thus, gated recursion trains on the same generated distribution as ungated recursion, but reweights samples by acceptance: high-r⁡(x,c)r(x,c) code receives more training mass, while low-r⁡(x,c)r(x,c) code is suppressed. At a fixed point of the gated recursion (pure self-training), one must satisfy

pθ∗​(c∣x)=qθ∗​(c∣x)⟺pθ∗​(c∣x)∝pθ∗​(c∣x)​r​(x,c),p_{\theta^{*}}(c\mid x)=q_{\theta^{*}}(c\mid x)\Longleftrightarrow p_{\theta^{*}}(c\mid x)\propto p_{\theta^{*}}(c\mid x)r(x,c), (2.8)

which implies that (for each xx) probability mass concentrates on the support where r⁡(x,c)r(x,c) is maximal (e.g., r⁡(x,c)=1r(x,c)=1 if such code exists). In contrast, the ungated recursion enforces only self-reproduction of its own samples and does not bias toward executability. This is why a useful exogenous gate can slow collapse, while a gate that becomes constant on the generator’s support loses its filtering effect and approaches ungated self-training.

2.2 Representation-Subspace Drift Under Recursive Self-Training

We next describe a representation-level view of recursive self-training collapse. Let 𝒟t\mathcal{D}_{t} denote the training distribution at iteration tt over prompt–code pairs (x,c)∈𝒳×𝒞(x,c)\in\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{C}, where 𝒟t\mathcal{D}_{t} may be ungated or gated. Fix a representation map

ϕ:𝒳×𝒞→ℝd,z:=ϕ⁡(x,c).\phi:\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{C}\to\mathbb{R}^{d},\qquad z:=\phi(x,c). (2.9)

The distribution 𝒟t\mathcal{D}_{t} induces a mean vector and covariance matrix in representation space:

μt:=𝔼(x,c)∼𝒟t​[z],Σt:=𝔼(x,c)∼𝒟t​[(z−μt)​(z−μt)⊤]∈ℝd×d.\mu_{t}:=\mathbb{E}_{(x,c)\sim\mathcal{D}_{t}}[z],\qquad\Sigma_{t}:=\mathbb{E}_{(x,c)\sim\mathcal{D}_{t}}\big[(z-\mu_{t})(z-\mu_{t})^{\top}\big]\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}. (2.10)

The covariance Σt\Sigma_{t} captures which representation directions remain diverse under the current training distribution. If recursive self-training narrows the generated code distribution, then Σt\Sigma_{t} should concentrate on fewer dominant directions.

Let Ut∈ℝd×kU_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times k} contain the top-kk eigenvectors of Σt\Sigma_{t}, and let Pt:=Ut​Ut⊤P_{t}:=U_{t}U_{t}^{\top} be the corresponding rank-kk projector. We measure consecutive subspace drift by

Sim⁡(t,t+1):=1k​Tr​(Pt​Pt+1)∈[0,1],Dist⁡(t,t+1):=‖Pt−Pt+1‖2=sin⁡θmax​(Ut,Ut+1).\mathrm{Sim}(t,t+1):=\frac{1}{k}\mathrm{Tr}(P_{t}P_{t+1})\in[0,1],\hskip 9.24994pt\mathrm{Dist}(t,t+1):=\|P_{t}-P_{t+1}\|_{2}=\sin\theta_{\max}(U_{t},U_{t+1}). (2.11)

Here, high similarity means the dominant representation subspace is stable, while large distance indicates that recursive training has shifted the main directions of variation.

To analyze the mechanism, we use a linearized covariance recursion:

Σt+1=A​Σt​A⊤,Σ0⪰0.\Sigma_{t+1}=A\Sigma_{t}A^{\top},\qquad\Sigma_{0}\succeq 0. (2.12)

This recursion should be read as a local approximation of how one round of retraining transforms representation covariance. Let A=U​diag​(s1,…,sd)​V⊤A=U\mathrm{diag}(s_{1},\ldots,s_{d})V^{\top} be an SVD with s1≥s2≥⋯≥sd≥0s_{1}\geq s_{2}\geq\cdots\geq s_{d}\geq 0. Then Σt=At​Σ0​(A⊤)t\Sigma_{t}=A^{t}\Sigma_{0}(A^{\top})^{t} and therefore

‖Σt‖2≤‖At‖22​‖Σ0‖2=s12​t​‖Σ0‖2.\|\Sigma_{t}\|_{2}\leq\|A^{t}\|_{2}^{2}\|\Sigma_{0}\|_{2}=s_{1}^{2t}\|\Sigma_{0}\|_{2}. (2.13)

More importantly, different singular directions are amplified at different rates. For any unit vector vv,

v⊤​Σt​v=‖(A⊤)t​v‖Σ02,‖(A⊤)t​v‖​scales as​sit​when ​v=vi.v^{\top}\Sigma_{t}v=\|(A^{\top})^{t}v\|_{\Sigma_{0}}^{2},\qquad\|(A^{\top})^{t}v\|\ \text{scales as}\ s_{i}^{t}\ \text{when }v=v_{i}. (2.14)

Thus, if s1≫s2s_{1}\gg s_{2}, the component aligned with the leading singular direction dominates after repeated retraining. Whenever Σ0\Sigma_{0} has nonzero energy in this direction, the ratio λ1​(Σt)/λ2​(Σt)\lambda_{1}(\Sigma_{t})/\lambda_{2}(\Sigma_{t}) is expected to increase with tt because the leading component is amplified roughly by s12​ts_{1}^{2t} while the next component is amplified roughly by s22​ts_{2}^{2t}. This gives a representation-space explanation for collapse: recursive self-training can progressively concentrate variance into a low-dimensional subspace, reducing diversity in the generated code distribution.

We now formalize the concentration effect by the linearized covariance recursion in Equation (2.12).

This gives a representation-level mechanism for mode concentration: the model distribution can become increasingly low-rank even while training continues to optimize self-generated samples.

2.3 Human Gate vs. AI Self-Gate

2.3.1 Verifier parameterization: exogenous Human gate vs. endogenous AI self-gate

We now specialize the generic acceptance function r⁡(x,c)r(x,c) from Equation (2.3). The key is whether the acceptance rule is fixed outside the generator or coupled to the generator during recursive training.

Human gate: exogenous acceptance.

A Human gate uses a fixed acceptance function rH​(x,c)∈[0,1]r_{H}(x,c)\in[0,1], rHr_{H} is independent of tt and θt\theta_{t}. It induces the accepted conditional distribution

qθtH​(c∣x):=pθt​(c∣x)​rH​(x,c)ZθtH​(x),ZθtH​(x):=∑c′∈𝒞pθt​(c′∣x)​rH​(x,c′).q^{H}_{\theta_{t}}(c\mid x):=\frac{p_{\theta_{t}}(c\mid x)r_{H}(x,c)}{Z^{H}_{\theta_{t}}(x)},\quad Z^{H}_{\theta_{t}}(x):=\sum_{c^{\prime}\in\mathcal{C}}p_{\theta_{t}}(c^{\prime}\mid x)r_{H}(x,c^{\prime}). (2.16)

The corresponding training distribution is mtH​(x,c)=pX​(x)​qθtH​(c∣x)m_{t}^{H}(x,c)=p_{X}(x)q^{H}_{\theta_{t}}(c\mid x). This covers model-independent review signals such as compilation, execution, quality checks, or human PR review.

AI self-gate: endogenous acceptance.

An AI self-gate uses a learned reviewer with parameters ϕt\phi_{t}, producing rϕt​(x,c)∈[0,1]r_{\phi_{t}}(x,c)\in[0,1]. It induces

qθt,ϕtA​(c∣x):=pθt​(c∣x)​rϕt​(x,c)Zθt,ϕtA​(x),Zθt,ϕtA​(x):=∑c′∈𝒞pθt​(c′∣x)​rϕt​(x,c′).q^{A}_{\theta_{t},\phi_{t}}(c\mid x):=\frac{p_{\theta_{t}}(c\mid x)r_{\phi_{t}}(x,c)}{Z^{A}_{\theta_{t},\phi_{t}}(x)},\quad Z^{A}_{\theta_{t},\phi_{t}}(x):=\sum_{c^{\prime}\in\mathcal{C}}p_{\theta_{t}}(c^{\prime}\mid x)r_{\phi_{t}}(x,c^{\prime}). (2.17)

The corresponding training distribution is mtA​(x,c)=pX​(x)​qθt,ϕtA​(c∣x)m_{t}^{A}(x,c)=p_{X}(x)q^{A}_{\theta_{t},\phi_{t}}(c\mid x). In our experiments, this case corresponds to perplexity filtering and binary self-scoring, where the code LLM evaluates its own generated samples. Unlike rHr_{H}, the score rϕtr_{\phi_{t}} can drift as the generator changes.

Taxonomy summary.

Table 1 classifies the six filtering strategies by whether the acceptance rule is exogenous or endogenous. Vanilla has no gate and accepts all generated code. Compile is a Human gate because it directly runs Python compilation and accepts code only when compilation succeeds. Quality is also a Human gate because it uses fixed code-quality rules, described in Section D, such as repetition rate and length. Compile+Quality combines these two model-independent rules, so it is also exogenous. Perplexity and Binary Classifier are AI self-gates: both use the code LLM itself to score its own generated code. Perplexity filters by the model’s own likelihood, while Binary Classifier uses the model’s own logit-difference score, defined in Section E. Since the generator also provides the filtering signal, these two gates are coupled to θt\theta_{t}.

Coupled dynamics under AI self-gating.

We now formalize the failure mode where the verifier is coupled to the generator. This captures the AI self-gate setting: the code LLM generates candidate code, scores its own outputs, and then trains on the samples it accepted. For a clean statement, we analyze the extreme case where the generator and verifier share the same parameters:

ϕt=θt,rϕt​(x,c)=rθt​(x,c).\phi_{t}=\theta_{t},\qquad r_{\phi_{t}}(x,c)=r_{\theta_{t}}(x,c). (2.18)
Assumption 2.2 (Self-confirming acceptance).

There exists a measurable function κ:𝒳→(0,1]\kappa:\mathcal{X}\to(0,1] such that for pXp_{X}-almost every xx, rθt​(x,c)=κ⁡(x)r_{\theta_{t}}(x,c)=\kappa(x) for pθt(⋅∣x)p_{\theta_{t}}(\cdot\mid x)-almost every cc.

Assumption 2.2 describes the rubber-stamp regime: on the code that the current model is likely to generate, the AI reviewer assigns essentially the same acceptance score. Once this happens, the gate no longer changes the training distribution.

Theorem 2.3 (Degeneracy to ungated recursion).

Assume the shared-parameter self-gate in Equation (2.18) and Assumption 2.2. Then for pXp_{X}-almost every xx,

Zθt,θtA​(x):=∑c′∈𝒞pθt​(c′∣x)​rθt​(x,c′)=κ⁡(x),Z^{A}_{\theta_{t},\theta_{t}}(x):=\sum_{c^{\prime}\in\mathcal{C}}p_{\theta_{t}}(c^{\prime}\mid x)r_{\theta_{t}}(x,c^{\prime})=\kappa(x), (2.19)

and for pθt(⋅∣x)p_{\theta_{t}}(\cdot\mid x)-almost every cc,

qθt,θtA​(c∣x):=pθt​(c∣x)​rθt​(x,c)Zθt,θtA​(x)=pθt​(c∣x).q^{A}_{\theta_{t},\theta_{t}}(c\mid x):=\frac{p_{\theta_{t}}(c\mid x)r_{\theta_{t}}(x,c)}{Z^{A}_{\theta_{t},\theta_{t}}(x)}=p_{\theta_{t}}(c\mid x). (2.20)

Consequently,

mtA​(x,c):=pX​(x)​qθt,θtA​(c∣x)=pX​(x)​pθt​(c∣x)=mtungated​(x,c)a.e.,m_{t}^{A}(x,c):=p_{X}(x)q^{A}_{\theta_{t},\theta_{t}}(c\mid x)=p_{X}(x)p_{\theta_{t}}(c\mid x)=m_{t}^{\mathrm{ungated}}(x,c)\qquad\text{a.e.}, (2.21)

and the gated MLE update coincides with the ungated self-training update:

arg⁡maxθ​𝔼(x,c)∼mtA​[log⁡pθ​(c∣x)]=arg⁡maxθ​𝔼(x,c)∼mtungated​[log⁡pθ​(c∣x)].\arg\max_{\theta}\mathbb{E}_{(x,c)\sim m_{t}^{A}}[\log p_{\theta}(c\mid x)]=\arg\max_{\theta}\mathbb{E}_{(x,c)\sim m_{t}^{\mathrm{ungated}}}[\log p_{\theta}(c\mid x)]. (2.22)

The proof is given in Appendix C. Theorem 2.3 states that once an AI self-gate becomes constant on the generator’s own support, filtering becomes mathematically identical to no filtering. This is exactly the recursive self-training failure case where the model writes code, approves its own code, and then trains on that approved code.

Corollary 2.4 (Collapsed fixed point).

If there exists (θ⋆,ϕ⋆)(\theta^{\star},\phi^{\star}) such that rϕ⋆​(x,c)≡1r_{\phi^{\star}}(x,c)\equiv 1 for all (x,c)(x,c), then for all xx,

qθ⋆,ϕ⋆A​(c∣x)=pθ⋆​(c∣x),mA​(x,c)=pX​(x)​pθ⋆​(c∣x).q^{A}_{\theta^{\star},\phi^{\star}}(c\mid x)=p_{\theta^{\star}}(c\mid x),\qquad m^{A}(x,c)=p_{X}(x)p_{\theta^{\star}}(c\mid x). (2.23)

Thus, the gating operator is the identity on pθ⋆(⋅∣x)p_{\theta^{\star}}(\cdot\mid x).

The proof is given in Appendix C.

2.3.2 When AI review matches human review: equivalence and a non-collapse condition

The previous theorem gives the failure case: self-confirming AI review degenerates to no review. We now give the non-collapse case: if AI review stays close to exogenous human review and the human gate accepts nonzero good-code mass, then AI-gated training remains close to human-gated training.

Uniform calibration error.

Recall the Human-gate conditional qθtHq^{H}_{\theta_{t}} in Equation (2.16) and the AI-self-gate conditional qθt,ϕtAq^{A}_{\theta_{t},\phi_{t}} in Equation (2.17). Here, rH​(x,c)r_{H}(x,c) denotes the human-style external review rule, while rϕt​(x,c)r_{\phi_{t}}(x,c) denotes AI review: the learned reviewer scores whether generated code should be accepted for future training. We measure how well the AI reviewer matches the human reviewer by the worst-case calibration error

εt:=supx∈𝒳,c∈𝒞|rϕt​(x,c)−rH​(x,c)|.\varepsilon_{t}:=\sup_{x\in\mathcal{X},c\in\mathcal{C}}\big|r_{\phi_{t}}(x,c)-r_{H}(x,c)\big|. (2.24)
Non-collapse human acceptance mass.

To avoid a degenerate case where almost no generated code is accepted by the human reviewer, we require the Human gate to accept a non-vanishing fraction of the generator’s probability mass.

Assumption 2.5 (Non-collapse human acceptance mass).

There exists z0∈(0,1]z_{0}\in(0,1] such that

ZθtH​(x)=∑c′pθt​(c′∣x)​rH​(x,c′)≥z0for ​pX​-almost every ​x​ and all ​t.Z^{H}_{\theta_{t}}(x)=\sum_{c^{\prime}}p_{\theta_{t}}(c^{\prime}\mid x)r_{H}(x,c^{\prime})\geq z_{0}\qquad\text{for }p_{X}\text{-almost every }x\text{ and all }t. (2.25)

Assumption 2.5 says that the external reviewer still finds enough acceptable code in the generator distribution. Without this lower bound, the accepted distribution can become unstable because it is normalized by a vanishing acceptance mass.

Quality gate sufficient condition.

A simple sufficient condition for Assumption 2.5 follows from the quality gate set ℱqual​(x)\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{qual}}(x). Suppose the human reviewer gives nontrivial acceptance probability to quality gate code: c∈ℱqual​(x)⟹rH​(x,c)≥δHc\in\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{qual}}(x)\Longrightarrow r_{H}(x,c)\geq\delta_{H} for some δH∈(0,1]\delta_{H}\in(0,1]. If the generator also assigns nontrivial mass to quality gate code, pθt​(ℱqual​(x)∣x)≥βHp_{\theta_{t}}\big(\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{qual}}(x)\mid x\big)\geq\beta_{H} for some βH>0\beta_{H}>0, then Assumption 2.5 holds with z0=δH​βHz_{0}=\delta_{H}\beta_{H}, since

ZθtH​(x)=∑c′pθt​(c′∣x)​rH​(x,c′)≥∑c′∈ℱqual​(x)pθt​(c′∣x)​rH​(x,c′)≥δH​pθt​(ℱqual​(x)∣x)≥δH​βH.Z^{H}_{\theta_{t}}(x)=\sum_{c^{\prime}}p_{\theta_{t}}(c^{\prime}\mid x)r_{H}(x,c^{\prime})\geq\sum_{c^{\prime}\in\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{qual}}(x)}p_{\theta_{t}}(c^{\prime}\mid x)r_{H}(x,c^{\prime})\geq\delta_{H}p_{\theta_{t}}\big(\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{qual}}(x)\mid x\big)\geq\delta_{H}\beta_{H}. (2.26)

Thus, the Human gate remains stable when it accepts quality gate code and the generator has not lost all probability mass on such code.

Theorem 2.6 (Uniform approximation of human-gated review).

Suppose the AI reviewer satisfies Equation (2.24) with εt<z0\varepsilon_{t}<z_{0}, and suppose Assumption 2.5 holds. Then for pXp_{X}-almost every xx,

∥qθt,ϕtA(⋅∣x)−qθtH(⋅∣x)∥1≤2​εtz0.\big\|q^{A}_{\theta_{t},\phi_{t}}(\cdot\mid x)-q^{H}_{\theta_{t}}(\cdot\mid x)\big\|_{1}\leq\frac{2\varepsilon_{t}}{z_{0}}. (2.27)

Consequently,

∥mtA−mtH∥1=∫𝒳pX(x)∥qθt,ϕtA(⋅∣x)−qθtH(⋅∣x)∥1dx≤2​εtz0.\big\|m_{t}^{A}-m_{t}^{H}\big\|_{1}=\int_{\mathcal{X}}p_{X}(x)\big\|q^{A}_{\theta_{t},\phi_{t}}(\cdot\mid x)-q^{H}_{\theta_{t}}(\cdot\mid x)\big\|_{1}dx\leq\frac{2\varepsilon_{t}}{z_{0}}. (2.28)

The proof is in Appendix C. Theorem 2.6 shows when AI review remains safe: the AI reviewer must stay close to human review, and the Human gate must accept nonzero generator mass. If εt\varepsilon_{t} grows or z0z_{0} shrinks, the bound weakens and AI review can approach ungated self-training.

Equivalently, AI-gated recursion avoids collapse only when εt≪z0\varepsilon_{t}\ll z_{0} and rH​(x,⋅)r_{H}(x,\cdot) is not approximately constant on supp(pθt(⋅∣x))\mathrm{supp}(p_{\theta_{t}}(\cdot\mid x)). These conditions mean that AI review remains calibrated to human review, and human review still separates good from bad generated code.

2.4 Quality Gate

The ideal gate for recursive code training would accept exactly the programs in the quality gate set ℱqual​(q)\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{qual}}(q): programs satisfying semantic correctness, runtime safety, efficiency, security/compliance, and readability requirements. We define this set and its quality dimensions (A)–(G) formally in Appendix D. In our experiments, Human-gate methods are concrete approximations to this ideal: the compile filter checks basic runtime validity, while the quality filter implements fixed code-quality rules such as repetition and length constraints. These model-independent checks remain stable as the generator degrades. In contrast, AI self-gates use model-derived scores that can drift with the generator, causing the gate to lose its connection to ℱqual​(q)\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{qual}}(q) as in Theorem 2.3.

3 Experiments

3.1 Evaluation Setup

Evaluation benchmarks.

We use three standard code generation benchmarks. HumanEval Chen et al. (2021); OpenAI (2021): 164 hand-written Python problems with 7–9 unit tests each; primary benchmark, metric = pass@1. MBPP Austin et al. (2021): 374 crowd-sourced introductory Python problems with 3 unit tests each (sanitized split); second primary benchmark. LiveCodeBench Jain et al. (2024): continuously updated competition problems that prevent data contamination; used as a robustness probe. We additionally report HumanEval+ and MBPP+ Liu et al. (2024) (augmented edge-case test suites) in per-round tables (Appendix H). All evaluations use bigcode-evaluation-harness Ben Allal et al. (2022) with temperature 0.8, top-pp 0.95; HumanEval+ and MBPP+ use the EvalPlus framework.

Base models.

We evaluate four code LLMs: SantaCoder (1.1B) Ben Allal et al. (2023) (HumanEval+ baseline: 0.171, MBPP+ baseline: 0.294), StarCoder2-3B Lozhkov et al. (2024) (HumanEval+ baseline: 0.274, MBPP+ baseline: 0.492), Qwen2.5-Coder-1.5B Hui et al. (2024) (HumanEval+ baseline: 0.372, MBPP+ baseline: 0.582), and Code Llama-7B Rozière et al. (2023) (HumanEval+ baseline: 0.287, MBPP+ baseline: 0.388). All five primary recursive regimes are evaluated on all four models for 5 recursive rounds.

Recursive pipeline.

At each round tt, model MtM_{t} generates synthetic code from a fixed prompt pool; the filtering gate (Human or AI self-gate; Table 1) selects 5,0005{,}000 accepted samples; Mt+1M_{t+1} is fine-tuned on the accepted set for 3,000 steps (so 5 rounds = 15k steps). Human gate methods generate in batches until 5,000 accepted; AI self-gate methods generate 20k once per round and retain the top/bottom 25%. All methods share the same optimizer, learning rate cosine schedule, and batch size—only the filtering policy differs. Hardware: NVIDIA RTX 6000 Ada Generation GPUs. Full implementation details are in Appendix J.

Filtering strategies.

We evaluate five primary regimes under the Human gate / AI self-gate taxonomy (Table 1). No gate: (1) Vanilla reuses all generated samples. Human gates: (2) Compile applies a syntax gate via compile(); (3) Quality applies fixed static metrics (repetition rate ≤0.3\leq 0.3, length ≥50\geq 50 tokens). AI self-gates: (4) Perplexity generates 20k samples and retains the lowest 25% by masked-completion perplexity; (5) Binary Classifier generates 20k samples and retains the top 25% by logit-difference score. Execution-validated training pipelines have been effective in code generation Le et al. (2022); Wei et al. (2024a); Gehring et al. (2025); Zheng et al. (2024); our experiments isolate the narrower question of whether such exogenous signals remain different from model-coupled self-review under recursive retraining. Extended Compile+Quality and Quality-20R trajectories are reported in Appendix H.

3.2 Main Collapse Results

Universal degradation.

Figure 2 is the central result of this paper. All four models decline from their pre-training baselines over 5 recursive rounds, even when generated code is filtered before reuse. This establishes the main empirical pattern: recursive self-training collapse persists across model families and gate types. Human gates generally preserve more executable and syntactically plausible code, especially early in the loop, while AI self-gates can select useful samples on HumanEval+ but become less reliable as their scoring distribution follows the generator.

Filter comparison at R1 and R5.

Figure 3 shows HumanEval+ pass@1 at Round 1 and Round 5 for each model and filter strategy. Binary filtering achieves the highest R5 HumanEval+ for SantaCoder (0.10370.1037), StarCoder2-3B (0.1220.122), and Qwen2.5-Coder (0.1220.122), while Compile filtering is best for Code Llama-7B (0.1710.171). However, higher R1 performance does not guarantee better R5 performance: for SantaCoder and StarCoder2, the binary classifier achieves the highest R1 score but shows more variable long-horizon behavior.

Heatmap of HumanEval+ across rounds.

Figure 4 provides a compact overview of all 20 model×\timesfilter combinations across rounds 1–5. Brighter cells indicate higher pass@1; the progressive darkening from left to right within each model block illustrates the general collapse trend. StarCoder2-3B with binary filtering achieves the highest round-1 score (0.1950.195) among all combinations, while Qwen2.5-Coder-1.5B with vanilla self-training collapses most severely, dropping to 0.0430.043 at Round 5.

3.3 SantaCoder: All Strategies Across Rounds

Main collapse result.

All strategies decline from the pre-retraining SantaCoder baseline (HumanEval+ 0.1710.171, MBPP+ 0.2940.294) across 5 recursive rounds. Figure 5 and Table 3 summarize the results. Vanilla collapses most severely: HumanEval+ falls from 0.0920.092 at R1 to 0.0730.073 at R5, while MBPP+ reaches 0.0080.008 at R4 and remains only 0.0190.019 at R5 (from baseline 0.2940.294; −93.5%-93.5\% at R5). Binary Classifier achieves the highest R5 HumanEval+ (0.1040.104) but shows erratic MBPP+ behavior, dropping to 0.0190.019 at R4. Quality filtering provides the most stable MBPP+ trajectory across rounds.

Per-round results for SantaCoder.

Table 2 reports HumanEval+, MBPP+, LiveCodeBench, and filter pass rate for SantaCoder across all five strategies and five rounds. Figure 6 complements the table by contrasting the early checkpoint with the extended SantaCoder checkpoint, making the short-horizon and long-horizon effects of each filter visible side by side.

Perplexity self-gating loses calibration.

Among all AI self-gate methods, perplexity filtering produces a more stable trajectory than binary classification on MBPP+. The filter pass rate for PPL slowly increases from 0.1670.167 at R1 to 0.2350.235 at R5 (Table 2), indicating gradual degradation of the self-calibration signal (Figure 7). This aligns with Theorem 2.3: once the generating model collapses, its perplexity signal becomes miscalibrated.

3.4 MBPP+ Collapse Pattern

MBPP+ degrades more severely than HumanEval+ across all models and filter strategies. Figure 8 shows MBPP+ trajectories for all models under all five filters. The most dramatic collapse is observed for SantaCoder under Vanilla self-training, where MBPP+ drops from the baseline 0.2940.294 to 0.0080.008 at Round 4 (−97.3%-97.3\%). Qwen2.5-Coder also collapses severely under Vanilla: MBPP+ from 0.5820.582 to 0.0820.082 at Round 5 (−85.9%-85.9\%). Code Llama-7B is notably more robust to MBPP+ collapse, with MBPP+ under Vanilla remaining at 0.2140.214 at Round 5, reflecting its stronger pretraining foundation.

3.5 LiveCodeBench: Near-Zero Collapse

Figure 9 shows LiveCodeBench pass@1 trajectories under the Vanilla filter for all four models. Despite Qwen2.5-Coder starting from the highest LCB baseline (0.2380.238), it collapses to 0.0000.000 by Round 5. Code Llama-7B starts at 0.0450.045 and reaches approximately 0.0030.003 at R5 under Vanilla. StarCoder2-3B and SantaCoder are already near zero throughout. This confirms that recursive self-training disproportionately degrades harder, out-of-distribution reasoning tasks even when introductory benchmarks show some residual performance.

3.6 Cross-Model Validation

We evaluate recursive self-retraining across all four code LLMs. Table 4 and Figure 10 confirm that vanilla recursive self-training collapse is a cross-model phenomenon.

Table 4 shows that recursive self-retraining causes consistent degradation across all model families. Vanilla collapses sharply: Qwen2.5-Coder drops from HumanEval+ 0.3720.372 to 0.0430.043 (−88.4%-88.4\%) and from MBPP+ 0.5820.582 to 0.0820.082 (−85.9%-85.9\%) by Round 5. Binary filtering is the best AI self-gate at R5 for SantaCoder (HumanEval+ 0.1040.104), StarCoder2-3B (HumanEval+ 0.1220.122), and Qwen2.5-Coder (HumanEval+ 0.1220.122). Code Llama-7B is an exception: Compile filtering is the best strategy at R5 (HumanEval+ 0.1710.171), showing that Human gate benefits depend on model and data characteristics.

3.7 Cross-Model Analysis

Figure 11 shows that both StarCoder2-3B and Qwen2.5-Coder-1.5B exhibit recursive self-training collapse regardless of filtering strategy, providing direct empirical corroboration that the collapse mechanism is not specific to SantaCoder.

Collapse magnitude.

Under vanilla self-retraining (no filter), StarCoder2-3B declines from a HumanEval+ baseline of 0.2740.274 to 0.1040.104 by round 5 (−62.0%-62.0\%) and from an MBPP+ baseline of 0.4920.492 to 0.1720.172 (−65.0%-65.0\%). Qwen2.5-Coder-1.5B collapses even more severely: HumanEval+ from 0.3720.372 to 0.0430.043 (−88.4%-88.4\%) and MBPP+ from 0.5820.582 to 0.0820.082 (−85.9%-85.9\%) by Round 5. Code Llama-7B shows the smallest collapse on HumanEval+ under Vanilla: from 0.2870.287 to 0.1340.134 (−53.3%-53.3\%), and on MBPP+ from 0.3880.388 to 0.2140.214 (−44.8%-44.8\%). The steeper decline in Qwen2.5-Coder is consistent with the stronger initial distribution hypothesis: a model pretrained on a richer code corpus exhibits a sharper distributional shift when contaminated with self-generated outputs.

Effect of filtering strategies.

The benefit of a gate depends on which failure mode the benchmark rewards. Compile filtering improves Qwen2.5-Coder at R5 relative to Vanilla on both HumanEval+ (0.0980.098 vs. 0.0430.043) and MBPP+ (0.1270.127 vs. 0.0820.082), and it is the strongest Code Llama-7B strategy on HumanEval+ (0.1710.171). For StarCoder2-3B, however, compile and quality filters lag behind Vanilla at R5 on HumanEval+ and MBPP+, showing that syntactic validity alone cannot guarantee semantic preservation. Binary filtering achieves the highest R5 HumanEval+ for three of four models, which means self-scoring can still rank some useful samples in early and medium horizons. Its MBPP+ behavior is weaker and less stable, matching our central story: AI self-gates may improve one visible metric while losing broader semantic coverage. Perplexity (PPL) filtering shows a slow increase in pass rate from approximately 0.170.17 to 0.240.24 (averaged across models; Figure 7), consistent with the endogenous degeneracy result of Theorem 2.3.

Collapse attractor.

Despite large differences in architecture size, pretraining data, and starting pass@1, all four models show qualitatively similar long-horizon degradation patterns. SantaCoder (0.1710.171 HumanEval+ baseline) and Qwen2.5-Coder (0.3720.372 baseline) both reach approximately 0.040.04–0.100.10 HumanEval+ pass@1 under Vanilla by Round 5. StarCoder2-3B and Code Llama-7B maintain somewhat higher residual performance (0.100.10–0.140.14), likely due to stronger capacity and pretraining data quality. This convergence to a common degradation floor is consistent with the theoretical prediction of a collapse attractor.

Key takeaway.

No filtering strategy evaluated here—Compile, Perplexity, Quality, or Binary—prevents collapse across all model families. Binary filtering achieves the best R5 HumanEval+ for three models, but this comes with erratic MBPP+ behavior. Human gates are more interpretable and preserve executable validity, yet simple compile/static filters are still too weak to guarantee semantic robustness. LiveCodeBench approaches near-zero for all models by Round 5 regardless of strategy, confirming that recursive self-training systematically degrades harder, out-of-distribution tasks.

4 Conclusion

We studied recursive self-training collapse in code LLMs under no review, Human-gate review, and AI-self-gate review. Across models and benchmarks, no review produces the sharpest degradation, Human gates preserve useful validity signals but cannot stop long-horizon semantic drift, and AI self-gates can look strong on early HumanEval-style metrics while their acceptance signal drifts with the generator. Our theory explains this through gated distributional reweighting: exogenous gates preserve an external quality signal, while endogenous gates can become self-confirming. Stable recursive code LLM training therefore needs verification that remains outside the model’s own preference distribution.

5 Limitations

Our experiments focus on Python benchmarks and models up to 7B parameters in the full five-strategy sweep, with additional StarCoder trajectories in the appendix. Human-gate filters are simplified proxies for full PR review and do not fully check semantics, security, or design quality. Longer horizons, larger models, multilingual code, stronger execution-based gates, and periodic human-verified data remain important future directions.

Appendix A Related Work

A.1 Model Collapse

The systematic study of model collapse begins with Shumailov et al. Shumailov et al. [2024], who demonstrate that training on recursively generated data causes (1) early collapse: distributional errors accumulate and the model drifts from the true distribution; and (2) late collapse: low-frequency events permanently disappear. Their experiments on VAE, GMM, and OPT confirm that fresh human data must be periodically injected to prevent collapse. Alemohammad et al. Alemohammad et al. [2023] study self-consuming image generation models, proving that pure synthetic training loops monotonically shrink distribution variance (MAD: Model Amplification Disorder). They identify three loop types: fully synthetic, augmented (partial human mixing), and accumulating (fixed replay); only augmented and accumulating loops with sufficient human fraction avoid collapse.

Briesch et al. Briesch et al. [2023] provide the first LLM-specific self-consuming study using logically verifiable outputs (logical expressions), finding that synthetic data fraction is the primary collapse predictor. Seddik et al. Seddik et al. [2024] apply random matrix theory: token variance decays exponentially per generation, and mixing ≥5%\geq 5\% real data prevents long-term collapse; 100%100\% synthetic data collapses linearly with generation count. Dohmatob et al. Dohmatob et al. [2024] reframe collapse as a change in scaling laws—synthetic training truncates the power-law tail of the data distribution, eliminating rare events. Suresh et al. Suresh et al. [2025] prove that preserving a fraction ϵ>0\epsilon>0 of real data per generation keeps the KL divergence from the true distribution bounded, while ϵ→0\epsilon\to 0 (pure synthetic) leads to unbounded divergence—formalizing the role of exogenous quality signal.

On the constructive side, Ferbach et al. Ferbach et al. [2024] prove a characterization theorem: self-consuming loops converge to the preference-maximizing distribution if and only if the curation function aligns with a ground-truth reward. This directly justifies our Human gate framework: a compile gate or execution gate aligns with ground-truth correctness; AI self-gate does not. Gillman et al. Gillman et al. [2024] propose a correction function that maps synthetic samples toward higher-probability regions of the true distribution, stabilizing loops; code execution is the natural correction function in the code domain. Zhu et al. Zhu et al. [2025] demonstrate token-level diversity perturbations as a mitigation strategy. Fu et al. Fu et al. [2025] introduce recursive stability conditions for Transformer in-context learning.

A.2 Modern Code Review and Exogenous Verification

Modern code review provides the software-engineering analogue of the Human gate in our framework. Bacchelli and Bird Bacchelli and Bird [2013] show that defect finding is only one part of review: reviewers also enforce design norms, share knowledge, and improve maintainability. Bosu et al. Bosu et al. [2015] study which review comments developers find useful, while McIntosh et al. McIntosh et al. [2016] link code-review coverage, participation, and reviewer expertise to post-release software quality. At industrial scale, Sadowski et al. Sadowski et al. [2018] describe Google’s tool-based review process over millions of changes. These studies motivate our abstraction of review as an exogenous acceptance rule: the important property is not that every decision is manual, but that acceptance is not produced by the same model distribution being retrained.

A.3 Code LLM Development

Representation era (2020–2021). CodeBERT Feng et al. [2020] established the bimodal NL-PL representation paradigm (encoder-only, 6 languages, MLM + RTD). Codex Chen et al. [2021] introduced generative code LLMs (12B, fine-tuned GPT on GitHub) and the pass@kk evaluation standard. AlphaCode Li et al. [2022] scaled to competition-level difficulty at 41B parameters, using massive sampling (10310^{3} candidates) plus execution-based filtering—an early Human gate.

Fill-in-the-middle and open-source (2022–2023). InCoder Fried et al. [2022] unified generation and infilling via causal masking. CodeGen Nijkamp et al. [2022] demonstrated multi-turn multi-lingual generation at 16B. The Stack Kocetkov et al. [2022] established 3TB permissive-license code as the community standard. SantaCoder Ben Allal et al. [2023] showed that 1.1B models with high-quality filtering can match much larger counterparts; this is our primary base model. StarCoder Li et al. [2023] (15.5B) set the open-source SOTA on HumanEval (67.2%). CodeT5+ Wang et al. [2023] demonstrated flexible encoder-decoder pretraining objectives.

Data-quality and instruction-tuning era (2023–2024). WizardCoder Luo et al. [2024] applied Evol-Instruct (AI-generated instruction evolution) to code, reaching HumanEval 57.3%; this is an early AI-assisted data augmentation pipeline. Gunasekar et al. Gunasekar et al. [2023] showed that 6B tokens of GPT-4-quality synthetic data can train a 1.3B model to HumanEval 50.6% (phi-1)—one-shot synthetic, not recursive. Magicoder Wei et al. [2024b] introduced OSS-Instruct: seed real code snippets →\to GPT-generated problems →\to 7B model at HumanEval 70.7%. StarCoder2 Lozhkov et al. [2024] and The Stack v2 extended to 900+ languages with improved governance. CodeRL Le et al. [2022] uses unit-test feedback and a learned critic for program synthesis, showing the value of grounding code generation in functional signals. SelfCodeAlign Wei et al. [2024a] introduced the first execution-validated self-alignment pipeline; its execution gate corresponds to our Human gate archetype. Code Llama Rozière et al. [2023] (7B, 13B, 34B) fine-tuned Llama 2 on code with a mixed code-language pretraining data mixture.

State-of-the-art (2024–2025). DeepSeek-Coder Guo et al. [2024] (1B–33B) achieves HumanEval 79.3% with repository-level training. DeepSeek-Coder-V2 Zhu et al. [2024] (MoE 236B/21B active) matches GPT-4-Turbo code ability. Qwen2.5-Coder Hui et al. [2024] (0.5B–72B) surpasses GPT-4o on LiveCodeBench at 72B. OpenCoder Huang et al. [2024] provides fully open recipe. OpenCodeInterpreter Zheng et al. [2024] integrates code generation with execution and refinement, further emphasizing executable feedback as an external training signal. RLEF Gehring et al. [2025] grounds code LLMs in execution feedback with RL, confirming execution-based reward is more stable than LLM-as-judge reward. DeepSeek-R1 DeepSeek-AI et al. [2025] demonstrates GRPO-based reasoning scaling with execution verification, reaching top-96th-percentile on Codeforces.

Appendix B Evaluation Benchmarks: Full Description

HumanEval.

Chen et al. Chen et al. [2021] introduce 164 hand-written Python programming problems with unit test suites. Each problem consists of a function signature, docstring, and 7–9 unit tests. The evaluation metric is pass@1 (using the unbiased estimator with n=200n=200 samples). HumanEval is the primary benchmark in this paper.

MBPP.

The Mostly Basic Programming Problems dataset Austin et al. [2021] contains 374 crowd-sourced Python problems focusing on introductory-level tasks (string manipulation, arithmetic, sorting). Each problem has 3 unit tests. We use the sanitized split. MBPP is our second primary benchmark.

LiveCodeBench.

LiveCodeBench Jain et al. [2024] continuously collects new programming problems from LeetCode, AtCoder, and Codeforces, preventing contamination from models that have been trained on earlier problems. In our experiments, SantaCoder achieves near-zero pass@1 on LiveCodeBench throughout retraining, reflecting the gap between introductory-level proficiency and competition-level reasoning. We retain it as a robustness probe.

HumanEval+ and MBPP+.

We additionally report HumanEval+ Liu et al. [2024] and MBPP+, which augment the original test suites with additional edge cases. Results are reported in all per-round tables.

Code generation metrics.

Table 5 summarizes common metrics for evaluating code generation quality.

SantaCoder: Open code LMs with governance and infilling-capable training.

The BigCode technical report on SantaCoder describes the development of 1.1B-parameter code LMs trained on permissively licensed data from The Stack with an emphasis on transparency and responsible release Ben Allal et al. [2023], Kocetkov et al. [2022]. The report studies deployment-relevant modeling choices, notably Multi-Query Attention (MQA) for faster decoder inference Shazeer [2019] and Fill-in-the-Middle (FIM) objectives that enable arbitrary-position code infilling Bavarian et al. [2022], Fried et al. [2022]. Evaluation is conducted using MultiPL-E, which extends unit-test-driven code generation benchmarks to many languages Cassano et al. [2022].

StarCoder: Open-access code LMs with long context, infilling, and responsible release.

StarCoder and StarCoderBase are 15.5B-parameter open-access code LMs trained primarily on permissively licensed data from The Stack Li et al. [2023], Kocetkov et al. [2022]. The models combine an 8K context window, Fill-in-the-Middle (FIM) training for infilling, and Multi-Query Attention (MQA) for faster large-batch decoding Li et al. [2023], Bavarian et al. [2022], Shazeer [2019].

StarCoder2: scaling open code LMs with The Stack v2.

StarCoder2 provides 3B/7B/15B parameter checkpoints trained on 3.3–4.3T tokens, incorporating Fill-in-the-Middle (FIM) training and fast decoder inference via multi-query style attention Lozhkov et al. [2024], Bavarian et al. [2022], Shazeer [2019].

Appendix D Quality Gate Set: Full Definition

D.1 Quality Dimensions for Code Solutions

Let qq denote a task/query and let 𝒟q\mathcal{D}_{q} be the induced input distribution (test-time instances) for qq. For a candidate program x∈𝒳x\in\mathcal{X}, let R⁡(x,i)R(x,i) denote the execution output on input i∼𝒟qi\sim\mathcal{D}_{q}, and let y⁡(q,i)y(q,i) denote the task-specific semantic ground truth. We define the following measurable quality dimensions, each of which can be used either as an evaluation metric or as a constraint in a quality gate set.

(A) Semantic correctness.

We quantify semantic success by the probability of producing the correct semantic output under 𝒟q\mathcal{D}_{q}:

mcorr(x;q):=Pri∼𝒟q[R(x,i)=y(q,i)].m_{\mathrm{corr}}(x;q):=\Pr_{i\sim\mathcal{D}_{q}}\bigl[R(x,i)=y(q,i)\bigr]. (D.1)

When only a reference answer is available (instead of y⁡(q,i)y(q,i)), the event R⁡(x,i)=y⁡(q,i)R(x,i)=y(q,i) can be replaced by “execution matches the reference after normalization.”

(B) Runtime safety (no crashes/undefined behavior).

Let 𝖢𝗋𝖺𝗌𝗁⁡(x,i)\mathsf{Crash}(x,i) be an indicator of runtime failure on input ii (e.g., uncaught exceptions, out-of-bounds access, non-termination detected by a timeout, or undefined behavior in low-level languages). We define

msafe​(x,q):=1−Pri∼𝒟q⁡[𝖢𝗋𝖺𝗌𝗁⁡(x,i)].m_{\mathrm{safe}}(x;q):=1-\Pr_{i\sim\mathcal{D}_{q}}\bigl[\mathsf{Crash}(x,i)\bigr]. (D.2)

Equivalently, one may impose a hard safety constraint:

Pri∼𝒟q⁡[𝖢𝗋𝖺𝗌𝗁⁡(x,i)]≤δsafe,\Pr_{i\sim\mathcal{D}_{q}}\bigl[\mathsf{Crash}(x,i)\bigr]\leq\delta_{\mathrm{safe}}, (D.3)

for a user-specified tolerance δsafe∈(0,1)\delta_{\mathrm{safe}}\in(0,1).

(C) Robustness to perturbations and distribution shift.

Let 𝒯⁡(i)\mathcal{T}(i) denote a set of admissible perturbations of an input ii (e.g., format variations, paraphrases, boundary-value modifications). We define robust correctness as

mrob(x;q):=Pri∼𝒟q[∀i′∈𝒯(i),R(x,i′)=y(q,i′)].m_{\mathrm{rob}}(x;q):=\Pr_{i\sim\mathcal{D}_{q}}\Bigl[\forall i^{\prime}\in\mathcal{T}(i),\ R(x,i^{\prime})=y(q,i^{\prime})\Bigr]. (D.4)

Alternatively, using a loss ℓ⁡(⋅,⋅)\ell(\cdot,\cdot), we define a worst-case risk:

ℛrob​(x,q):=𝔼i∼𝒟q​[supi′∈𝒯⁡(i)ℓ⁡(R⁡(x,i′),y⁡(q,i′))].\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{rob}}(x;q):=\mathbb{E}_{i\sim\mathcal{D}_{q}}\Bigl[\sup_{i^{\prime}\in\mathcal{T}(i)}\ell\bigl(R(x,i^{\prime}),y(q,i^{\prime})\bigr)\Bigr]. (D.5)
(D) Resource usage and efficiency.

Let T⁡(x,i)T(x,i) be the runtime cost (e.g., wall-clock time) and optionally M⁡(x,i)M(x,i) the memory footprint or C⁡(x,i)C(x,i) the number of external API calls. A simple efficiency score is the negative expected runtime:

mres​(x,q):=−𝔼i∼𝒟q​[T⁡(x,i)].m_{\mathrm{res}}(x;q):=-\mathbb{E}_{i\sim\mathcal{D}_{q}}\bigl[T(x,i)\bigr]. (D.6)

One may also enforce probabilistic latency constraints:

Pri∼𝒟q[T(x,i)≤τ]≥1−δtime,\Pr_{i\sim\mathcal{D}_{q}}\bigl[T(x,i)\leq\tau\bigr]\geq 1-\delta_{\mathrm{time}}, (D.7)

or tail-latency bounds (e.g., the 0.990.99-quantile):

Quantile0.99​(T⁡(x,i))≤τ0.99.\mathrm{Quantile}_{0.99}\bigl(T(x,i)\bigr)\leq\tau_{0.99}. (D.8)
(E) Security and compliance.

Let 𝖡𝖺𝖽⁡(x,i)\mathsf{Bad}(x,i) indicate unsafe or policy-violating behavior (e.g., invoking dangerous system calls, writing to sensitive paths, unintended network access, or insecure deserialization). We define

msec​(x,q):=1−Pri∼𝒟q⁡[𝖡𝖺𝖽⁡(x,i)],m_{\mathrm{sec}}(x;q):=1-\Pr_{i\sim\mathcal{D}_{q}}\bigl[\mathsf{Bad}(x,i)\bigr], (D.9)

or impose a hard constraint Pr⁡[𝖡𝖺𝖽]≤δsec\Pr[\mathsf{Bad}]\leq\delta_{\mathrm{sec}} for δsec∈(0,1)\delta_{\mathrm{sec}}\in(0,1).

(F) Maintainability and testability.

Maintainability can be captured by static code metrics such as cyclomatic complexity, code duplication, and dependency burden:

mmaint​(x):=−(λ1​Cyclomatic​(x)+λ2​Dup​(x)+λ3​Deps​(x)),m_{\mathrm{maint}}(x):=-\Bigl(\lambda_{1}\mathrm{Cyclomatic}(x)+\lambda_{2}\mathrm{Dup}(x)+\lambda_{3}\mathrm{Deps}(x)\Bigr), (D.10)

with weights λ1,λ2,λ3≥0\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2},\lambda_{3}\geq 0. If a unit-test distribution 𝒯unit\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{unit}} is available, test pass rate provides an executable proxy:

mtest​(x):=Prt∼𝒯unit⁡[x​passes test​t].m_{\mathrm{test}}(x):=\Pr_{t\sim\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{unit}}}\bigl[x\ \text{passes test}\ t\bigr]. (D.11)
(G) Readability and style (including documentation consistency).

Let Sread​(x)∈[0,1]S_{\mathrm{read}}(x)\in[0,1] be a readability/style score from either rule-based or learned evaluators. We set

mread​(x):=Sread​(x).m_{\mathrm{read}}(x):=S_{\mathrm{read}}(x). (D.12)

When inline documentation doc⁡(x)\mathrm{doc}(x) is present, one may additionally measure documentation–implementation consistency via an alignment score Align⁡(x,doc⁡(x))\mathrm{Align}\bigl(x,\mathrm{doc}(x)\bigr), where larger values indicate better semantic agreement.

D.2 Quality-Feasible Code Set

Let qq denote a task/query, 𝒳\mathcal{X} the program space, and 𝒟q\mathcal{D}_{q} the input distribution induced by qq. Let V:𝒳→{0,1}V:\mathcal{X}\to\{0,1\} be a feasibility verifier, R⁡(x,i)R(x,i) the execution result of program xx on input ii, and y⁡(q,i)y(q,i) the task-specific semantic ground truth. We further define runtime event predicates 𝖢𝗋𝖺𝗌𝗁⁡(x,i)\mathsf{Crash}(x,i) (crash/exception/undefined behavior) and 𝖡𝖺𝖽⁡(x,i)\mathsf{Bad}(x,i) (unsafe or policy-violating behavior), a runtime cost T⁡(x,i)T(x,i) (e.g., wall-clock time), and a readability/style scorer Sread​(x)∈[0,1]S_{\mathrm{read}}(x)\in[0,1]. For user-specified thresholds δsafe,δsec∈(0,1)\delta_{\mathrm{safe}},\delta_{\mathrm{sec}}\in(0,1) and τ,r0>0\tau,r_{0}>0, we define the quality-feasible solution set as

ℱqual(q):={x∈𝒳\displaystyle\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{qual}}(q):=\Bigl\{x\in\mathcal{X} :V⁡(x)=1⏟feasibility,\displaystyle:\underbrace{V(x)=1}_{\text{feasibility}}, (D.13)
Pri∼𝒟q[R(x,i)=y(q,i)]≥δcorr⏟semantic correctness,\displaystyle\underbrace{\Pr_{i\sim\mathcal{D}_{q}}\bigl[R(x,i)=y(q,i)\bigr]\geq\delta_{\mathrm{corr}}}_{\text{semantic correctness}},
Pri∼𝒟q⁡[𝖢𝗋𝖺𝗌𝗁⁡(x,i)]≤δsafe⏟runtime safety,\displaystyle\underbrace{\Pr_{i\sim\mathcal{D}_{q}}\bigl[\mathsf{Crash}(x,i)\bigr]\leq\delta_{\mathrm{safe}}}_{\text{runtime safety}},
𝔼i∼𝒟q​[T⁡(x,i)]≤τ⏟resource/efficiency,\displaystyle\underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{i\sim\mathcal{D}_{q}}\bigl[T(x,i)\bigr]\leq\tau}_{\text{resource/efficiency}},
Pri∼𝒟q⁡[𝖡𝖺𝖽⁡(x,i)]≤δsec⏟security/compliance,\displaystyle\underbrace{\Pr_{i\sim\mathcal{D}_{q}}\bigl[\mathsf{Bad}(x,i)\bigr]\leq\delta_{\mathrm{sec}}}_{\text{security/compliance}},
Sread​(x)≥r0⏟readability/style},\displaystyle\underbrace{S_{\mathrm{read}}(x)\geq r_{0}}_{\text{readability/style}}\Bigr\},

where δcorr∈(0,1]\delta_{\mathrm{corr}}\in(0,1] specifies the minimum acceptable semantic success rate. If only a reference answer is available (rather than y⁡(q,i)y(q,i)), the event R⁡(x,i)=y⁡(q,i)R(x,i)=y(q,i) can be replaced by “execution matches the reference after normalization.”

D.3 Supporting Assumptions

Assumption D.1 (Non-trivial quality-feasible completeness / coverage).

Let 𝒟\mathcal{D} denote the target distribution over queries qq, and for each qq let 𝒟q\mathcal{D}_{q} be the induced input distribution. Let V:𝒳→{0,1}V:\mathcal{X}\to\{0,1\} be a feasibility verifier and define the quality gate set ℱqual​(q)⊆𝒳\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{qual}}(q)\subseteq\mathcal{X} as in the main text (incorporating feasibility, semantic correctness, runtime safety, efficiency, security/compliance, and readability/style). Then for 𝒟\mathcal{D}-almost every query qq, there exists a non-empty subset ℱqual​(q)\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{qual}}(q) and constants α,β∈(0,1]\alpha,\beta\in(0,1] such that

μ⁡(ℱqual​(q))≥α,Pθ0​(ℱqual​(q)∣q)≥β,\mu\bigl(\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{qual}}(q)\bigr)\geq\alpha,\qquad P_{\theta_{0}}\bigl(\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{qual}}(q)\mid q\bigr)\geq\beta, (D.14)

where μ\mu is a reference measure on 𝒳\mathcal{X} (or on the relevant solution equivalence class for qq), and Pθ0(⋅∣q)P_{\theta_{0}}(\cdot\mid q) is the initial generator’s conditional distribution.

Assumption D.2 (Quality-feasible margin).

Let d:𝒳×𝒳→ℝ≥0d:\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0} be a metric (or pseudometric) on 𝒳\mathcal{X}, and define

d⁡(x,ℱqual​(q)):=infy∈ℱqual​(q)d⁡(x,y).d(x,\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{qual}}(q)):=\inf_{y\in\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{qual}}(q)}d(x,y). (D.15)

There exists γ>0\gamma>0 such that for 𝒟\mathcal{D}-almost every qq, for all x∈ℱqual​(q)x\in\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{qual}}(q) and all x′∈𝒳x^{\prime}\in\mathcal{X},

d⁡(x,x′)≤γ⟹x′∈ℱqual​(q).d(x,x^{\prime})\leq\gamma\Longrightarrow x^{\prime}\in\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{qual}}(q). (D.16)

Equivalently, the γ\gamma-ball around any x∈ℱqual​(q)x\in\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{qual}}(q) is contained in ℱqual​(q)\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{qual}}(q).

Assumption D.3 (Local contraction toward the quality gate set).

Let C:𝒳→𝒳C:\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{X} denote a correction (or calibration) operator applied to candidate programs. There exist constants ρ∈(0,1)\rho\in(0,1) and η≥0\eta\geq 0 such that for 𝒟\mathcal{D}-almost every qq and all xx in the region of interest,

d⁡(C⁡(x),ℱqual​(q))≤ρ​d​(x,ℱqual​(q))+η.d\bigl(C(x),\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{qual}}(q)\bigr)\ \leq\ \rho\,d\bigl(x,\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{qual}}(q)\bigr)\ +\ \eta. (D.17)

When η=0\eta=0, CC is a strict contraction toward ℱqual​(q)\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{qual}}(q); when η>0\eta>0, the term η\eta captures an irreducible residual error (noise floor).

Appendix E AI Self-Verification Protocol

E.1 Implemented AI Self-Gates

This appendix details the two AI self-gate methods used in our experiments: Perplexity and Binary Classifier. We use these methods as representative AI self-verification protocols because both derive acceptance scores from the code LLM itself, rather than from human labels, execution tests, or external static analyzers. Thus, the same model family that generates candidate code also evaluates which samples enter future training.

Basic formulation.

Let qq denote the programming problem and let xx denote a code sample generated by the current code LLM. We construct an evaluation prompt Πeval​(q,x)\Pi_{\mathrm{eval}}(q,x) that contains the problem statement, the candidate code, and an explicit request for assessment. The model then produces an evaluation response

r∼pθ​(r∣Πeval​(q,x)).r\sim p_{\theta}(r\mid\Pi_{\mathrm{eval}}(q,x)). (E.1)

This is a self-evaluation procedure because the same parameterized model pθp_{\theta} first generates xx and then, under a different prompt or scoring rule, evaluates xx.

Binary-classifier self-gate.

The binary self-gate forces the model into a two-label judgment. The evaluation prompt asks the model to classify a candidate as good or bad. In our implementation, the prompt appends “\n# quality: ” to the last 2000 tokens of the generated completion. The acceptance score is

Sbin​(x∣q)=log⁡Pθ​(good∣q,x)−log⁡Pθ​(bad∣q,x).S_{\mathrm{bin}}(x\mid q)=\log P_{\theta}(\texttt{good}\mid q,x)-\log P_{\theta}(\texttt{bad}\mid q,x). (E.2)

Samples are ranked by Sbin​(x∣q)S_{\mathrm{bin}}(x\mid q), and the top 25% are retained for the next round of recursive fine-tuning. This uses only the model parameters: no human label, execution result, or external quality metric is used.

Perplexity self-gate.

Code LLMs are generative models trained to predict code tokens and are commonly used for code completion or masked/fill-in-the-middle generation. We therefore use the model’s own conditional likelihood as an AI self-gate. For each generated sample xx under problem context qq, we compute

Sppl(x∣q)=−1|x|∑i=1|x|logPθ(xi∣q,x<i).S_{\mathrm{ppl}}(x\mid q)=-\frac{1}{|x|}\sum_{i=1}^{|x|}\log P_{\theta}(x_{i}\mid q,x_{<i}). (E.3)

Equivalently, the perplexity is

PPLθ​(x∣q)=exp⁡(Sppl​(x∣q)).\mathrm{PPL}_{\theta}(x\mid q)=\exp\big(S_{\mathrm{ppl}}(x\mid q)\big). (E.4)

Generated samples with lower Sppl​(x∣q)S_{\mathrm{ppl}}(x\mid q), or lower PPLθ​(x∣q)\mathrm{PPL}_{\theta}(x\mid q), are treated as more acceptable. In our implementation, samples are ranked by perplexity and the lowest 25% are retained for future training. This is an AI self-gate because the same code LLM family generates xx through completion/filling and then scores xx by its own token likelihood.

E.2 Other Candidate AI Self-Verifier Protocols

The following protocols are natural extensions of AI self-verification, but are not used as main filtering methods in our experiments.

Chain-of-thought judge followed by forced verdict.

A stronger AI verifier can first generate an assessment trace and then output a forced final verdict. The evaluation prompt may request the model to summarize the intended algorithm, identify possible bugs or edge-case failures, and then output a final label from a fixed set. The model generates a reasoning trace zz and a verdict yy:

pθ(y,z∣q,x)=pθ(z∣q,x)pθ(y∣q,x,z).p_{\theta}(y,z\mid q,x)=p_{\theta}(z\mid q,x)p_{\theta}(y\mid q,x,z). (E.5)
Self-consistency over judge samples.

Since one judge response can be noisy, the model can sample multiple evaluations:

r(1),r(2),…,r(M)∼pθ(⋅∣Πeval(q,x)).r^{(1)},r^{(2)},\dots,r^{(M)}\sim p_{\theta}(\cdot\mid\Pi_{\mathrm{eval}}(q,x)). (E.6)

The final self-judgment can be obtained by majority vote,

y^vote​(x∣q)=mode⁡{y(1),…,y(M)},\hat{y}_{\mathrm{vote}}(x\mid q)=\operatorname{mode}\{y^{(1)},\dots,y^{(M)}\}, (E.7)

or by averaged label probabilities:

y^avg​(x∣q)=arg⁡maxy∈𝒴​1M​∑m=1MPθ(m)​(y∣q,x).\hat{y}_{\mathrm{avg}}(x\mid q)=\arg\max_{y\in\mathcal{Y}}\frac{1}{M}\sum_{m=1}^{M}P_{\theta}^{(m)}(y\mid q,x). (E.8)
Constrained multi-label judge.

For code LLMs, the evaluation prompt should be constrained. A weak prompt such as “Is this code good?” is underspecified. A more controlled prompt asks the model to check whether the implementation matches the specification, handles corner cases, and avoids likely bugs, then end with exactly one label from a fixed set such as CORRECT, LIKELY_CORRECT, UNCERTAIN, LIKELY_BUGGY, or BUGGY. This still remains an AI self-gate if the score is produced by the same model family that generated the code.

Why AI self-evaluation degrades.

LLM evaluators exhibit significant self-preference bias Panickssery et al. [2024]: they assign higher scores to outputs in their own generation style, regardless of actual quality. As the model collapses and its style converges to a narrow distribution, the evaluator’s preferences converge with it, causing the gate to accept progressively worse outputs with progressively higher confidence. This is the self-confirming regime formalized in Assumption 2.2 and Theorem 2.3. For production-quality judging protocols that mitigate this bias, see Panickssery et al. [2024], Hashemi et al. [2024], Zheng et al. [2023].

Appendix F Mixed Training

Code LLMs differ in their pretraining data mixtures, and we adapt the recursive fine-tuning format accordingly. The key distinction is whether a model was trained mainly on raw source code or on a broader mixture of code and code-related natural language.

SantaCoder.

SantaCoder Ben Allal et al. [2023] is pretrained on Python, Java, and JavaScript from The Stack Kocetkov et al. [2022]. Its data consists primarily of source-code files, with natural language appearing only inside comments, docstrings, and identifiers. We therefore fine-tune SantaCoder using pure code samples in the recursive loop.

StarCoder and StarCoder2.

StarCoder Li et al. [2023] and StarCoder2 Lozhkov et al. [2024] are trained on broader code corpora that include source code together with code-related natural language, such as issues, commits, pull-request text, and notebook content. For these models, recursive fine-tuning uses a mixed code–natural-language format to better match the original training distribution.

Qwen2.5-Coder.

Qwen2.5-Coder Hui et al. [2024] follows a multi-stage code-model training pipeline, including large-scale code pretraining, code-related natural-language data, and instruction tuning. We therefore also use a mixed code–natural-language fine-tuning format for Qwen2.5-Coder rather than pure code-only retraining.

Training mixture used in our experiments.

Following the model-specific formats above, we use pure-code recursive fine-tuning for SantaCoder and mixed code–natural-language fine-tuning for StarCoder, StarCoder2, and Qwen2.5-Coder. For the mixed setting, each round uses approximately 70–80% code and 20–30% code-related natural language, including problem statements, comments, commits, issues, notebooks, and instruction-style descriptions. After recursive data construction, the accepted samples are used for SFT-style fine-tuning, and we preserve a small human-verified or execution-verified anchor set when available. When recursive retraining is applied, Human-gate runs use model-independent checks such as compilation and quality rules at every round, while AI-self-gate runs use model-assigned scores such as PPL. This design follows prior analyses of recursive training collapse Suresh et al. [2025], Seddik et al. [2024] and code-model training practice Gunasekar et al. [2023], while keeping the controlled variable fixed: within each model family, only the review policy changes.

Appendix G Compile Error Analysis

Figure 12 and Table 6 report the compile and execution-pass analysis of generated code under vanilla recursion and the compile-based Human gate. We evaluate 500 generated samples with a 5s timeout. Adding the Human gate substantially increases the relaxed pass rate: vanilla drops from 55.4% at R1 to 34.6% at R5, while compile filtering maintains a much higher relaxed pass rate of 88.2% at R1 and 89.4% at R10. The error distribution also changes sharply. Under vanilla recursion, the “Other error” category grows from 42.8% to 64.2%, indicating increasing runtime failure. In contrast, the compile-based Human gate keeps “Other error” low, from 9.2% at R1 to 7.4% at R10. This shows that even a simple exogenous compile gate significantly improves executable validity and prevents runtime-error proliferation.

Appendix H Per-Round Degradation Trajectories (SantaCoder, All Strategies)

Figure 13 reports the per-round degradation trajectories of all six filtering strategies on SantaCoder. Each panel corresponds to one strategy and shows HumanEval pass@1 and MBPP pass@1 across recursive retraining rounds. Dotted horizontal lines denote the pre-retraining baseline for each benchmark. Quality-20R is evaluated for 20 rounds with sparse checkpoints to study long-horizon behavior, while the other strategies are evaluated for 5–10 rounds.

Figure 13 shows that all strategies degrade below the pre-retraining baseline as recursive training proceeds. Vanilla collapses rapidly without any filtering, while Human-gate strategies generally preserve higher scores for longer. Quality-20R remains more stable over long horizons than the AI-self-gate methods. In contrast, Binary Classifier reaches a high early MBPP score but then drops sharply, matching the self-confirming gate failure described in Theorem 2.3.

Appendix I Cross-Model Degradation Trajectories

This section reports cross-model degradation trajectories under vanilla recursion, Human-gate filtering, and AI-self-gate filtering. Figure 14 compares filtering strategies on StarCoder2-3B and Qwen2.5-Coder-1.5B. Figure 15 further reports compile-gated runs and extended vanilla trajectories.

Figures 14 and 15 show that recursive self-training collapse is not specific to SantaCoder. Under vanilla recursion, all model families fall far below their pre-retraining baselines, with Qwen2.5-Coder dropping fastest despite starting from the highest baseline. Human-gate filtering can delay degradation, especially in the early rounds, but it does not fully prevent long-horizon decline. AI-self-gate filtering by PPL is also unstable: it remains below the pretraining baseline and often underperforms compile or quality filtering on MBPP. Overall, the cross-model results support the same conclusion as the main SantaCoder experiments: no review collapses fastest, Human gates slow collapse, and AI self-gates do not reliably stop recursive degradation.

Figure 16 compares vanilla recursive self-training across three code LLM families. All models degrade rapidly from their step-0 pretraining baseline on both HumanEval and MBPP. Qwen2.5-Coder starts from the highest baseline but collapses the fastest, dropping sharply within the first few retraining steps. SantaCoder also falls quickly and reaches low scores after only a few rounds. StarCoder degrades more slowly than the smaller models, but it still remains far below its initial baseline after extended retraining. These results show that larger or stronger code models may slow the collapse rate, but vanilla recursive self-training still causes consistent long-horizon degradation.

Appendix J Implementation Details

Data generation and filtering.

At each recursive round, the current model first performs one inference pass to generate candidate code from the fixed prompt pool. The accepted set size is fixed to 5000 samples per round. For Human-gate methods, we generate samples in batches of 2000 until 5000 samples pass the filter. For AI-self-gate methods, we generate 20,000 samples once, score all candidates, and retain the top or bottom 25% depending on the score definition. After the accepted set is built, the model is fine-tuned on these self-generated samples for 3000 training steps. Thus, 10 recursive rounds correspond to 30k training steps. Across methods, the recursive loop is the same: one generation stage followed by one fine-tuning stage per round; only the filtering policy differs.

Evaluation and hardware.

After each round, all methods are evaluated on HumanEval Chen et al. [2021], OpenAI [2021], MBPP Austin et al. [2021], and LiveCodeBench Jain et al. [2024]. We use bigcode-evaluation-harness Ben Allal et al. [2022] with temperature 0.8 and top-pp 0.95 for generation, and greedy decoding for final pass@1 computation. HumanEval+ and MBPP+ are evaluated with EvalPlus Liu et al. [2024]. For execution-pass analysis, we evaluate 500 generated samples with a 5s timeout. All experiments are conducted on NVIDIA RTX 6000 Ada Generation GPUs.
